chunks: Ali ibn Mahziyar narrated from Fadala ibn Ayyub, from al-Husayn ibn Uthman, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Basir, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who stood up for prayer and forgot to say the Takbir, so he began with the recitation. He said: 'If he remembers it while standing before he bows, let him say the Takbir; and if he has bowed, let him continue in his prayer.'

This report is also like the previous two, because the implied meaning of the speech in the report is: 'If he remembers it while standing before he bows, let him say the Takbir; and if he bows without remembering it, let him continue in his prayer.' And the report does not state that if he bows while remembering that he did not say the Takbir, he should continue in his prayer; and our interpretation does not contradict what we presented earlier.
The Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) said: And if he left the recitation out of forgetfulness, there is no requirement for him to repeat it.

key_terms.التَّكْبِير: Saying 'Allahu Akbar' (God is the Greatest), specifically the opening Takbir in prayer
key_terms.الْقِرَاءَة: Recitation of the Quran during prayer

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a person forgets the opening Takbir or the recitation during prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from the *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of *nasi* (forgetfulness) regarding the opening Takbir, establishing a pragmatic distinction between remembering while standing versus after bowing. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on preserving the continuity of prayer (*istiqra'*) rather than imposing rigid repetitions for minor omissions, a principle further supported by the Sheikh al-Tusi’s note that forgetting recitation entirely does not invalidate the prayer. This ruling underscores the juristic preference for ease (*taysir*) in ritual acts when errors are unintentional.
